sections.h2: What sets St. Johns County apart in the Census data?
sections.html:
Income and schooling stand out. The Census Bureau puts median household income for 2020 to 2024 at $109,839 and per capita income at $57,346, with 50.9 percent of adults 25 and older holding a bachelor's degree and 5.8 percent of residents below the poverty line. Owners occupy 82.2 percent of the 115,794 households, and the midpoint owner home is valued at $489,200.

Growth is the other story. The county went from 190,039 people in 2010 to 273,425 in 2020 and reached an estimated 346,328 by mid-2025, up 26.7 percent on the 2020 base. Permits hit 4,735 in 2025, and the average commute is 26.9 minutes. Owners with a mortgage report a median monthly cost of $2,351, against $728 for those without one, which shows how much of the carrying cost for a newer buyer is the loan and not the tax. All figures are from Census QuickFacts.

sections.h2: What does the St. Johns County property appraiser give a new owner?
sections.html:
A checklist, and a few useful phone numbers. The office's new owner page opens with a note that the county runs from farmland to beaches, then tells buyers to find the parcel's record card, complete the sales questionnaire and verify the name and mailing address, because the TRIM notice and bill go to that address. A button on the record card estimates the tax bill.

  • Customer service: 904-827-5500.
  • Business equipment returns: 904-827-5508.
  • Building department: 904-827-6800.
  • Planning and zoning: 904-209-0675.
  • Utility department: 904-209-2700.

The page also sends owners to the tax collector to update a Florida driver license, a step that matters because the homestead application checks that the license shows the homestead address. New business owners may need a local business tax application and must create an account with the appraiser.

sections.h2: Which dates does the St. Johns County appraiser publish?
sections.html:
The important dates page runs through the year, and the dates change what a seller or buyer can claim.

  • January 1: the status of the property sets its value for the assessment year, and ownership and residence on this day decide homestead eligibility.
  • January 1 to April 1: business equipment returns are filed.
  • March 1: filing closes for homestead, other personal exemptions, classified use, agricultural classification and organizational exemptions.
  • August and September: TRIM notices go out with proposed assessments, millage and hearing dates.
  • November: the tax collector mails bills.

A weekend March 1 pushes the cutoff to Monday, and the homestead page named March 2 for 2026.

sections.h2: What is the 2026 homestead figure in St. Johns County, and who qualifies?
sections.html:
The appraiser prints $51,411 for the 2026 tax year, now indexed to inflation. A first block of $25,000 applies to every levy, school bills among them. The remaining $26,411 applies to assessed value between $50,000 and $75,000 and leaves school tax untouched.

To qualify, an owner must be a Florida permanent resident who holds title and lives in the home on January 1. Neither spouse may take a residency-based exemption in another state, and the office wants proof of that. Applicants bring a Florida license or ID showing the homestead address and Social Security numbers for both spouses, which are required for online filing. A noncitizen needs a Permanent Resident Card. If you owned a Florida home before, give its address or parcel number. Closing after January 1 means that year's exemption is out of reach.

Once approved, the owner need not reapply unless marital status, ownership or title changes. A late application for just cause can be filed through the end of the TRIM period, which usually falls late in August.

sections.h2: Can a St. Johns County homeowner rent the house and keep homestead?
sections.html:
Renting a portion is fine; renting all of it is limited. The appraiser says the part of a home not rented stays eligible, and a garage apartment or other separate rental space can be carved out while the rest keeps the exemption. Renting the whole property for more than 30 days in two consecutive tax years ends it, and a rental lasting over six months in a tax year is presumed commercial.

Ownership structure matters too. Property held in a trust qualifies if the applicant is the trustee or the trust language gives beneficial title. Moving the house into an LLC or another business entity is treated as a change of ownership, which strips every exemption and cap. After a divorce or marriage, the appraiser may ask for a new application, and it sends notice when the deed is recorded in St. Johns County. A deed recorded elsewhere leaves the owner responsible for telling the office.

sections.h2: How does portability work in St. Johns County?
sections.html:
Portability lets an owner carry the gap between market and assessed value, up to $500,000, from one Florida homestead to another. The move must happen within three tax years, counted January through December from the sale, and a December sale counts as one tax year.

The appraiser adds several rules. Downsizing is allowed, and the transferable amount shrinks in proportion to the lower value of the new home. Everyone who owned the old home and owns the new one must apply together, and each spouse of a married couple counts. Portability can be used any number of times but never from outside Florida. Spouses who abandon a jointly titled home may split the difference with Form DR-501TS, provided they were married on the abandonment date. The benefit total appears on the TRIM notice and the record card for a St. Johns County home. Non-homestead property carries a separate 10 percent cap, and that benefit cannot be ported.

sections.h2: Which other exemptions does St. Johns County list, and what proof do they need?
sections.html:
All of the breaks below are due by March 1 and the office asks applicants to visit in person. Dollar amounts are the ones the appraiser prints.

Selected personal exemptions on the St. Johns County appraiser's page
ExemptionAmountProof asked for
Age 65 or older, limited incomeUp to $50,000Form DR-501SC and prior year household income
Widowed$5,000Mark it on the homestead form or give the death certificate
Blind$5,000Form DR-416 or DR-416B, or SSDI proof
Totally and permanently disabled civilian$5,000Form DR-416 or SSDI letter
Veteran disabled 10 percent or more$5,000DD-214 and a VA disability letter
Combat-related disabled veteran, 65 or olderEqual to the disability ratingForm DR-501DV, DD-214, VA letter

Source: St. Johns County Property Appraiser, other exemptions. The same page lists total exemptions for quadriplegics, for certain permanent disabilities with limited income, for veterans totally and permanently disabled through service, for surviving spouses of those who died on active duty and for first responders disabled in the line of duty, plus a deployment exemption on Form DR-501M. Churches, schools, hospitals, nursing homes, affordable housing and historic buildings fall under property-use exemptions. With 23,534 veterans and 22.5 percent of residents 65 or older, many sellers qualify for something here.

sections.h2: How does a St. Johns County owner dispute a value?
sections.html:
Start with a conversation at the appraiser's office; if that fails, a petition goes to the Value Adjustment Board. The TRIM notice goes out in mid-August. A petition may be filed within 25 days of that mailing, and the date is printed at the top of the notice itself.

The Clerk of the Circuit Court and County Comptroller manages the process and posts the petition form, at 904-819-3600. The appraiser's site carries a Value Adjustment Board page and a Property Owner Bill of Rights. A denied exemption, classification or portability claim has its own 30 day window under state guidance, so a seller who thinks the assessment is too high should act before listing.

sections.h2: What do state rules add when a St. Johns County house sells?
sections.html:
Stamp tax is seventy cents on each hundred dollars of price and binds every party named on the deed. The clerk charges $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each after it. Debt that stays on the house is counted in the price.

Unpaid bills turn delinquent April 1, certificates are sold by June 1, and a holder may apply for a deed after two years, with half the latest assessed value added to the opening bid on homestead land. Get a payoff from the collector and have the title company search for certificates.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 homestead exemption total in St. Johns County?
faqs.a: $51,411, per the appraiser's homestead page. The first $25,000 reaches all levies and $26,411 applies to value between $50,000 and $75,000, excluding school taxes.

faqs.q: Is the March 1 homestead deadline ever different in St. Johns County?
faqs.a: Yes, when March 1 falls on a weekend the filing moves to the next business day. The office listed March 2 for 2026.

faqs.q: Does a St. Johns County buyer keep the seller's capped value?
faqs.a: No. A sale resets the home to market value the next January 1. The seller may port up to $500,000 of the gap to a new Florida homestead within three tax years.

faqs.q: Can I rent my whole St. Johns County homestead for a few months?
faqs.a: Renting the entire home for more than 30 days in two consecutive tax years ends the exemption. A rental beyond six months in one year is presumed commercial.

faqs.q: Who runs the Value Adjustment Board paperwork in St. Johns County?
faqs.a: The circuit clerk and comptroller, at 904-819-3600. A petition is due 25 days after TRIM notices are mailed.
